documents: Wu et al. (2022) Active Nitrogen Cycle Driven by Solar Radiation in Clean Desert Air, Earth's Future 10, e2021EF002451 (published PDF, 10 pages)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (identical to the printed 'n of 10' journal pages); supplementary material cited by figure number (S1-S8) because the supplement was not supplied

entry.evidence: this release and the consequent response of the nitrogen cycles in desert air have not been evaluated

sequences.source_document: Wu et al. 2022, Earth's Future, published PDF

steps.action: The authors cite their own earlier daily aerosol data from the Taklimakan Desert, which showed stable nitrate concentrations higher than in remote marine and forest air.
steps.quote: revealed relatively stable nitrate concentrations that were much higher than those typically encountered in remote marine and tropical forest air

steps.action: They propose that reactive N emitted from desert soils may drive active N cycling in desert air.
steps.quote: may initiate the active cycling of nitrogen compounds in desert air

steps.action: They pose three aims: the diurnal variation of nitrate in clean desert air, its governing mechanisms, and its broader implications.
steps.quote: we investigated nitrate in a desert environment, with a focus on (a) the diurnal variations of nitrate in clean desert surface air

steps.action: They chose a sampling site on an active dune at the NE rim of the Tengger Desert, barren on three sides, with a village and a city to the east.
steps.quote: The south, west, and north directions of the site are totally barren

steps.action: In four short campaigns (2014-2016, spring, summer, autumn) they collected HNO3 (nylon filter) and particulate nitrate (Teflon filter) at 1.5 m in 2-3 hr intervals, with particle counts and meteorology, and analysed the filters by ion chromatography.
steps.quote: were collected 1.5 m above the desert sand dunes at a time resolution of 3 hr

steps.action: About 10% field blanks were used to set detection limits (3 SD of blanks) and to propagate uncertainty; filter-pack positive artifacts were argued to be minor from the literature and thermodynamics.
steps.quote: The value of three times the standard deviation of the blank values was used as a measure of significance

steps.action: They screened out samples likely affected by anthropogenic sources using wind sector and speed, the fine/coarse particle ratio, SO4/Ca, and K/Ca (fixed threshold 0.1, plus Hampel MED+3MAD outlier criteria).
steps.quote: Data screening was implemented to exclude samples that likely contained pollutants emitted from local and regional anthropogenic sources.

steps.action: They established that total nitrate shows daytime increases and nighttime decreases in all seasons, with summer highest, from 74 screened samples.
steps.quote: displayed clear diurnal variations with increases during the daytime and decreases during the nighttime

steps.action: A Student's t-test of day versus night means showed significant differences in summer only; spring and autumn differences were not significant.
steps.quote: were not significant (p > 0.05) because of their low concentrations.

steps.action: They compared the concentrations with other desert studies and remote ecosystems: within the ranges seen in other deserts, comparable to remote continental sites, and higher than remote marine and forest sites.
steps.quote: is considerably higher than in remote marine and forest areas

steps.action: From the day/night pattern they hypothesize photochemical formation of HNO3 (NO2 + OH, with OH from O3 photolysis).
steps.quote: t-nitrate very likely formed through photochemical reactions

steps.action: They fitted an exponential relation between background HNO3 and ERA-Interim surface soil temperature as a proxy for solar radiation (r2 = 0.53).
steps.quote: We indirectly confirmed the dependence of the HNO3 concentration on solar radiation (Figure 2)

steps.action: Using a cited deposition velocity and a residual-layer height, they estimated a dry-deposition loss of about 10% per hour, enough to explain the nighttime HNO3 decrease.
steps.quote: which could account for almost all nighttime nitric acid loss

steps.action: Two summer simulations, one without the N2O5 pathway and one without HNO3 photolysis, showed that both pathways have little effect on HNO3.
steps.quote: both pathways have little effect on atmospheric HNO3

steps.action: Correlating NO3- with NH4+ showed full neutralization, so NH4NO3 is the main particulate form; the opposite daytime trends were attributed to temperature-driven NH4NO3 dissociation.
steps.quote: indicating that NH4NO3 was the primary form

steps.action: From the seasonality (summer > spring > autumn), they argued that photolytic conversion of particulate nitrate to HONO is not a major control on the cycle.
steps.quote: it is not greatly affected by the photolytic conversion of particulate nitrate into HONO

steps.action: Their HNO3 was about twice the 1997-2009 HNO3 at the WMO GAW Waliguan background station, which they ascribed to abundant local precursor gases from surface emissions.
steps.quote: approximately twice these values, indicating that there were abundant precursor gases at the desert site

steps.action: They rejected direct mineral-dust nitrate as the source: dust peaks in spring, but nitrate peaked in summer.
steps.quote: its concentration should have been the highest in spring

steps.action: Citing published estimates, they rejected lightning and stratospheric intrusions as sufficient sources.
steps.quote: those sources could not account for the nitrate level we observed in the desert air

steps.action: From the literature they list candidate soil N emission mechanisms: nitrification, denitrification, chemodenitrification, high-temperature oxidation, subsurface nitrate pools, biocrusts, deposited-nitrate photolysis, and saline lakes.
steps.quote: High soil-surface temperatures (greater than 50°C), driven by solar radiation, can cause nitrogen loss in desert soils.

steps.action: They ran WRF-CHEM (6 km, MOZART boundaries, MEGAN, Behrendt et al. 2014 soil NO scheme) for the observation periods, with and without desert soil NO emission, to compute the HNO3 each scenario predicts.
steps.quote: the WRF-CHEM model was run for the observation periods to investigate the relationships between the NOx soil emissions and atmospheric HNO3

steps.action: Checked WRF soil temperature against field observations at the Shapotou desert station: consistent.
steps.quote: soil temperature from the WRF model was very consistent with those of the field observations

steps.action: Because WRF significantly overestimated soil moisture, they fixed it at the observed Shapotou mean of 0.05.
steps.quote: We set the soil moisture level to a fixed value of 0.05

steps.action: Compared the simulated with the observed August 2014 HNO3. With soil emission the model gave a pronounced diurnal cycle with a larger amplitude than observed; without soil emission it gave only a slight variation. Modelled fluxes were 0.2-0.7 ng m-2 s-1.
steps.quote: for the model run without any local HNO3 soil emissions, there was a very slight diurnal variation

steps.action: They rejected regional transport as the cause of the observed diurnal variation.
steps.quote: These results suggest that regional transport could not account for the observed diurnal variations

steps.action: A box model with NO emissions only was used to check that the observed nitrate trend can be reproduced.
steps.quote: the results show that the trend of nitrate we observed in clean desert air could be largely reproduced

steps.action: They keep the claim of a diurnal nitrate cycle in clean desert air, driven by solar-radiation-induced surface N emission coupled with photochemistry.
steps.quote: Our results demonstrate the existence of a diurnal nitrate cycle in clean desert air

steps.action: They analysed July-September 2018 satellite NO2 columns (OMI, OMPS, GOME-2A/B) over the Taklimakan, North American, Saharan, Middle Eastern, and Australian deserts, which showed daytime increases.
steps.quote: clear increases in the column NO2 concentration with solar heating during the daytime in the desert air

steps.action: They extend the claim: NOx oxidation efficiency is higher in desert air than in other remote ecosystems, and deserts may be important for ozone production and regional or global ozone budgets.
steps.quote: Our findings indicate that the NOx oxidation efficiency in the desert air is significantly higher than in other remote ecosystems.

tree.answer: A diurnal nitrate (HNO3 + NO3-) cycle in clean desert air
Nitrate is observed directly by filter packs; soil emissions and photochemistry are not measured, only modelled
Explain the mechanism of the diurnal variation and its implications
Rivals: direct dust nitrate, lightning or stratospheric NO, regional transport, particulate-nitrate photolysis, N2O5 and photolysis pathways
Yes: dust predicts a spring maximum; transport predicts no diurnal cycle in the no-soil-emission model run
Found: four field campaigns in natural conditions

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats over seasons and years, and across deserts worldwide in satellite NO2
Partly: day/night difference significant only in summer; generalization by satellite; model ablations
Soil emission plus photochemical oxidation kept as the best explanation

end.claim: Clean desert air in the Tengger Desert carries an active diurnal nitrate cycle, produced by solar-radiation-induced reactive-N emission from desert soils followed by photochemical oxidation to HNO3.

decisive_move.sentence: Only the WRF-CHEM run with desert soil NO emission produced a diurnal HNO3 cycle of observed (or larger) amplitude, while the run without it did not; this attributes the cycle to soil emission rather than regional transport.

gates.evidence: Action: the introduction states the expectation that desert soil N emission may drive active cycling (p. 2), and the nitrate campaigns were designed around it, but the sampling is generic monitoring. Claim: the no-emission model run could have reproduced the cycle and did not (p. 7), and the dust rival made a seasonal prediction that failed (p. 6). However, day/night differences are significant only in summer (p. 5), and the with-emission model overestimates the amplitude with no skill score. Registration: screening criteria (K/Ca < 0.1 from Wu et al. 2017) were set from prior work, but nothing indicates the hypothesis or analysis was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Hampel (1985) robust outlier detection (median + 3 MAD) for data screening
Student's t-test of day versus night means
Ion chromatography (Dionex ICS-1100) for filter extracts
Behrendt et al. (2014) soil NO release parameters for the Mongolian Desert, used in the emission scheme

novelty_claims.quote: We found a considerable but not widely known response of atmospheric nitrogen cycle to the emission of reactive nitrogen compounds from desert soils
these points have not been taken into account so far in any climate models
An active diurnal cycle of nitrogen compounds driven by solar radiation was found in clean air at a Chinese desert

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the supplement was not supplied, so steps citing Figures S2-S8 rely on the main-text descriptions. No NO, NO2, HONO, O3 or soil flux was measured at the site; the soil-emission mechanism rests on modelling and literature. The observational record is short (14-30 screened samples per season), and the day/night difference is significant only in summer (t-nitrate is not significant in any season, Table 1). The model comparison is shown only for August 2014; the with-emission run overestimates the amplitude, and no quantitative score is given. The box-model setup is not described. Campaign dates in Table 1 (April 20-25, 2015; October 23-26, 2016) differ from the text (April 10-13; October 10-13), and the satellite period is given as '1 July to 31 September 2018'. Inference: the satellite step compares instruments with different overpass times and does not separate soil NO from other NO2 sources, so it supports generalization only weakly. Sub-claims at other statuses: the worldwide occurrence of similar desert cycles is a possibility, best_explanation at most ('possible similar cycles'). The higher NOx oxidation efficiency and the role of deserts in ozone production are not tested (status none). The HNO3-soil temperature relation is regularity_in_range, using reanalysis soil temperatures the authors note are biased.

disagreements.support: Measured nitrate levels exceeding remote marine and forest air, the Waliguan comparison, and the WRF-CHEM soil-emission runs indicate that desert N emission drives an active cycle that should be included.
disagreements.quote: they have often been overlooked in air-surface N exchange estimates at the global scale

disagreements.target: Studies showing small soil NOx fluxes in deserts (Hartley & Schlesinger, 2000; McCalley & Sparks, 2009)
disagreements.support: High t-nitrate despite small fluxes is interpreted as high NOx oxidation efficiency in desert air; this is not measured directly.
disagreements.quote: although studies always showed that soil NOx fluxes in the desert were small
